title: State Pattern
tagline: Let an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes — as if it changed its class.

sections.content:
Every non-trivial object lives through a lifecycle. An `Order` is created, then paid, then shipped, then delivered. A TCP socket starts closed, moves through SYN_SENT and ESTABLISHED, and eventually settles in TIME_WAIT. A media player is either stopped, playing, or paused. The naive way to handle these lifecycles is with a single `status` field and a forest of `if`/`switch` blocks: every method begins with `if (this.status === 'pending') { ... } else if (this.status === 'paid') { ... }`. This seems harmless for two states. But systems grow. At five states and ten methods, the switch-case soup contains fifty branches — and adding a sixth state means editing every method, risking regressions in logic you did not intend to touch.

The **State pattern** is the GoF (Gang of Four) answer: move each state's behaviour into its own **State class**. The **Context** (your `Order`, your `TrafficLight`, your `TcpConnection`) holds a reference to the *current* state object and delegates every action to it. When a transition fires, the Context swaps its state reference. The same method call — `order.ship()` — now produces completely different behaviour depending on which state object is currently installed. The Context stays clean and stable; only the installed state changes.

This chapter builds the pattern from first principles: the problem statement with before/after code, the full participant structure, a class diagram and state machine diagram, real JavaScript implementations with edge cases, the difference between State and its close cousin Strategy, when to use a library instead of rolling your own, and the misconceptions that trip up even experienced engineers.

sections.title: A Vending Machine with Physical State Compartments
sections.content:
Imagine a vending machine with a mechanical dial that physically clicks into one of four positions: **Idle**, **HasCoin**, **Dispensing**, and **OutOfStock**. Each dial position activates a different set of electrical contacts — a completely different circuit.

When you insert a coin in the **Idle** position, the machine clicks the dial to **HasCoin**. Pressing a product button in **HasCoin** advances the dial to **Dispensing** and triggers the motor. Once the product drops, the dial returns to **Idle** (or **OutOfStock** if inventory is zero).

Here is the key insight: **the button labelled 'Select Product' is always the same button**. What changes is which circuit it connects to based on the dial position. In the **Idle** position that button does nothing; in **HasCoin** it dispenses; in **OutOfStock** it plays a 'sorry' tone.

The State pattern works exactly this way. The Context (vending machine body) is always the same object with the same public interface. The current state object (the dial position) decides what each call actually does. Adding a 'Maintenance' state means building a new circuit board — you do not rewire the existing ones.

sections.title: The Problem in Full: Life Before the State Pattern
Participants: Context, State Interface, ConcreteStates
sections.content:
The pattern has three roles:

**State (interface or abstract class)** declares all action methods the Context exposes. In JavaScript this is a duck-typed contract: any object that implements `pay(ctx)`, `ship(ctx)`, `cancel(ctx)`, and `name()` qualifies as a state. In TypeScript you would use an `interface OrderState { pay(ctx: Order): void; ... }`. The interface forces every ConcreteState to handle every possible action — no gaps.

**ConcreteState** implements the State interface for one specific lifecycle position. It contains only the logic relevant to that state. Crucially, it receives the Context as a parameter in every method call (`pay(ctx)`) — this handle allows the state to call `ctx.setState(new PaidState())` and trigger the transition. Each ConcreteState is a small, focused class of ~15–25 lines, independently readable and testable.

**Context** (`Order`, `TrafficLight`, `TcpSocket`) is the object clients interact with. It holds `this._state` (the current ConcreteState) and exposes public methods that are nothing but forwarding calls: `pay() { this._state.pay(this); }`. The Context also exposes `setState(newState)` which the ConcreteStates call to advance the machine. The Context may optionally perform entry/exit side effects in `setState` (logging, event emission, persistence hooks).

**Data that belongs in Context vs. State:** The current state object should be *stateless* — it carries no instance data beyond perhaps singleton-style caching. All the domain data (`order.id`, `order.total`, `order.customerId`) belongs in the Context. This is important: ConcreteStates are often safe to share across Context instances as singletons (lazy-initialised static references), avoiding object allocation on every transition.

sections.title: State Transition Diagrams: Making the Machine Explicit
sections.content:
One of the biggest wins of the State pattern is that it forces you to draw — and then encode — the exact transition graph before you write a line of logic. A state machine has:

- **States** — the finite set of configurations the object can be in (Pending, Paid, Shipped, Cancelled)
- **Events** — the operations that can be invoked (pay, ship, cancel)
- **Transitions** — which event in which state leads to which next state
- **Guard conditions** (optional) — predicates that must be true for a transition to fire (e.g., `ship()` from Paid is guarded by `stock > 0`)
- **Actions** (optional) — side effects executed on entry to a state (send confirmation email) or on a specific transition (deduct inventory)

Drawing this diagram *before* coding reveals illegal transitions immediately. In the Order machine: `ship()` from `Pending` is illegal (no payment yet). `pay()` from `Shipped` is a no-op. `cancel()` from `Shipped` is either a no-op or triggers a return-shipping workflow — a business decision that must be made explicit.

The State pattern enforces this clarity because each ConcreteState *must* implement *every* method. You cannot accidentally leave a transition undefined; you are forced to write the handler and make the decision: transition, warn, throw, or no-op.

sections.title: State-Driven vs Context-Driven Transitions
State vs. Strategy: A Critical Distinction
sections.content:
State and Strategy are structurally near-identical — both replace a conditional with a polymorphic object. Developers regularly confuse them. The distinction is semantic and architectural, not syntactic.

**Strategy:** The pattern for *interchangeable algorithms*. A `Sorter` may use a `BubbleSortStrategy` or a `QuickSortStrategy`. The strategies are independent — they do not know about each other, do not transition to each other, and the same strategy can be reused across any number of contexts without meaning. The Context selects a strategy based on an external decision.

**State:** The pattern for *lifecycle phases of an object*. States form a **directed graph** — they know about and transition to each other. `PendingState` transitions to `PaidState`; `PaidState` transitions to `ShippedState` or `CancelledState`. States are specific to the Context's lifecycle; you would not reuse `PaidState` in an unrelated `Document` object. The transitions are *internally driven* by events on the Context itself, not chosen externally.

A useful test: if you could swap Strategy A for Strategy B at any time and the program would still make sense, it is a Strategy. If swapping states in the wrong order would violate invariants (paying a cancelled order, shipping before paying), it is a State machine.

Another angle: **Strategy replaces a single algorithm**; **State replaces a whole family of related behaviours that belong to one lifecycle**. The difference matters for architecture — State pattern implies you need to draw a state diagram; Strategy implies you need a selection policy.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Strategy Pattern"] --> B["Algorithms are\ninterchangeable"]
    A --> C["No transitions\nbetween strategies"]
    A --> D["Context selects\nalgorithm externally"]
    E["State Pattern"] --> F["States form\na directed graph"]
    E --> G["States trigger\neach other"]
    E --> H["Object drives\nown lifecycle"]
sections.caption: State vs Strategy: both delegate behaviour, but only State creates a graph of interdependent phases. Strategy is about selecting an algorithm; State is about modelling an object lifecycle.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Singleton states avoid allocation on every transition — critical when orders are processed at high throughput. The onEnter hook centralises side effects (email, logging) so they fire for every transition into a state, not just specific ones. The stock guard in PaidState.ship() demonstrates how guard conditions prevent illegal transitions without throwing exceptions.

sections.title: TypeScript: Typing the Pattern Correctly
When to Reach for XState Instead
sections.content:
The hand-rolled State pattern is excellent for machines with 3–6 states and straightforward transitions. But real applications hit scaling walls:

**Parallel states** — a `Delivery` can be simultaneously tracking GPS and managing driver assignment. These are orthogonal sub-machines that run in parallel. Hand-rolling this is extremely complex; XState models it natively.

**Hierarchical states (nested)** — a `Loading` state might have sub-states `ConnectingToServer`, `TransferringData`, `DecompressingResponse`. Hierarchical state machines (HSMs) let child states inherit transitions from parent states. Without a library, you implement this with nested state objects and brittle delegation chains.

**History states** — when leaving a complex nested state, you often want to return to the same sub-state you were in. XState has a `history` pseudo-state for this. By hand, you need to persist the last sub-state explicitly.

**Guards as pure functions** — XState makes guards first-class: `{ target: 'shipped', guard: ({ context }) => context.stock > 0 }`. They are separated from state behaviour and can be composed and tested independently.

**Devtools and visualization** — XState's visualizer renders the state machine diagram from the code definition. The diagram *is* the code. This is invaluable for communicating machine logic to non-engineers.

**Serialization** — XState machines can snapshot their current state to a plain object and restore it. Perfect for persisting order state to a database or resuming a wizard form.

The rule of thumb: if you are drawing a diagram with more than 6 states, or you need parallel regions, hierarchy, or devtools — reach for XState (JavaScript/TypeScript) or a similar library (Statecharts.io, Robot, Zag.js). Hand-roll only when you want zero dependencies and have a well-bounded, simple machine.

sections.caption: Decision tree for choosing between a plain flag, a hand-rolled State pattern, and a statechart library. Complexity drives the choice upward.

sections.content:
**Real-world examples of the State pattern in production systems:**

- **TCP/IP socket lifecycle** (RFC 793): CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RECEIVED → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED. This is arguably the most famous finite state machine in computer science — 11 states with 15+ transitions. Linux implements it explicitly in `net/ipv4/tcp.c`.
- **React `useReducer`**: the reducer function is a state machine — `(state, action) => nextState`. The `status` field inside the state object maps to ConcreteState classes; dispatched action types map to events. Redux Toolkit's `createAsyncThunk` uses `pending`, `fulfilled`, `rejected` status strings — textbook State pattern terminology.
- **XState** powers UI workflows in major applications including Microsoft Office Online (document editing workflows), Stately (state machine design tool), and numerous form wizard implementations.
- **Game AI** state machines: idle → patrol → chase → attack → flee. Unity's Animator Controller is a visual state machine editor that compiles to a State pattern.
- **Order Management Systems** (Shopify, commercetools, BigCommerce): every order has an explicit status lifecycle. commercetools's API exposes state transitions as first-class REST resources — you POST to `/orders/{id}/transitions` to advance the state machine.

**When to use the State pattern:**
- An object's behaviour changes substantially based on an internal `status` field
- You have 3+ states with non-trivial logic in each
- You need auditable, explicit transitions (for logging, debugging, or compliance)
- You need to add new states without modifying existing ones (open/closed principle)
- You want to test each state's behaviour in isolation

**When NOT to use the State pattern:**
- A simple boolean flag (`isOpen`, `isLoading`) controls trivial behaviour — do not create two state classes for on/off
- Only one or two methods behave differently; `if` is cleaner than a full pattern
- The transitions are entirely external (e.g., a theme toggle chosen by the user) — Strategy is the right pattern
- You need parallel states, hierarchy, or serialization — use XState rather than extending the hand-rolled pattern

**Common misconceptions:**
- 'State means Redux state or React state' — no. The State *pattern* is specifically about the GoF behavioural pattern where an object delegates method calls to swappable state objects.
- 'Each state class needs to import all other state classes' — only in the State-driven model. The hybrid return-based model avoids all cross-imports.
- 'State is only for OOP' — functional state machines (reducers, pattern-matching on a union type) are equally valid implementations of the same concept.

items: **Core idea:** Move each state's behaviour into its own ConcreteState class. The Context holds a reference to the current state and forwards all calls to it — `pay() { this._state.pay(this); }`. Swapping the state object changes all behaviour at once.
**Eliminates shotgun surgery:** Adding a new state means adding one class. No existing state class or Context method needs to change — the open/closed principle is fully satisfied.

**State vs Strategy:** Strategy provides interchangeable algorithms with no awareness of each other. State creates a directed graph of lifecycle phases that transition to each other — states know about sibling states.

**Transitions can be State-driven** (ConcreteState calls `ctx.setState(new NextState())`) or **Context-driven** (a central transition table maps event+currentState → nextState). State-driven is the GoF canonical form; Context-driven scales better for large machines.
**Entry and exit actions** centralise side effects (email, logging, events) per state rather than per transition — fire once whenever a state is entered, regardless of which transition triggered it.
**Singleton states** (one instance shared across all Contexts) eliminate allocation overhead and are safe when ConcreteStates carry no instance data of their own.

**Scale threshold:** Hand-roll for 3–6 states with simple transitions. Use XState or a statechart library when you need parallel states, nested states, serialization, history, or visualization tooling.

quiz.question: What is the primary structural problem that the State pattern solves?
options: Objects having too many public methods exposed to clients.
A growing if/switch thicket where every method branches on the same status field — making it impossible to add a new state without editing all methods.
Preventing multiple objects from sharing the same state simultaneously.
Ensuring database transactions are rolled back when an error occurs.
quiz.explanation: The naive approach puts status-based if/switch in every method. Adding a new state requires editing all methods — shotgun surgery. State moves each state's logic into its own class so new states are additions, not modifications.

quiz.question: In the GoF State pattern, how does the Context's pay() method typically look?
options: A 20-line switch statement covering all possible statuses.
An async method that queries a database for the current state.
A single delegation line: this._state.pay(this).
A static factory method that returns a new Order in the paid state.
quiz.explanation: After applying the State pattern, every Context method becomes a one-line delegation to the current state object. All the branching logic moves into ConcreteState classes.

quiz.question: Why does a ConcreteState method receive the Context (e.g., ctx or order) as a parameter?
options: So the state can access private fields of the Context that are otherwise inaccessible.
So the state can call ctx.setState(nextState) to trigger a transition from within the state object.
So multiple Context instances can share the same ConcreteState without confusion.
To satisfy the interface requirement — the parameter is never actually used.
quiz.explanation: In the State-driven (GoF canonical) model, the ConcreteState calls ctx.setState(new NextState()) to advance the machine. Without the Context reference, the state can only act — it cannot transition.

quiz.question: What is the key architectural difference between the State pattern and the Strategy pattern?
options: Strategy uses inheritance; State uses composition.
State classes form a directed graph — they know about and transition to each other. Strategy algorithms are fully independent of each other.
Strategy is only for synchronous operations; State works asynchronously.
State is a creational pattern; Strategy is a structural pattern.
quiz.explanation: State classes are interdependent: PendingState knows about PaidState and transitions to it. Strategy algorithms are isolated — BubbleSortStrategy has no knowledge of QuickSortStrategy. This graph vs independence distinction is the defining difference.

quiz.question: What is an 'entry action' in the context of state machines?
options: A guard condition that must be true before a transition fires.
A side effect (email, log, event) executed every time a particular state is entered, regardless of which transition triggered it.
The constructor logic run when a new ConcreteState object is instantiated.
A method that returns the previous state to allow undo functionality.
quiz.explanation: Entry actions fire on every arrival into a state. Placing 'send confirmation email' in ShippedState.onEnter() means it fires whether you arrived from PaidState or any other transition — no duplication across multiple transition handlers.

quiz.question: Why are singleton ConcreteState instances (one object shared across all Contexts) often a safe optimisation?
options: Singletons prevent race conditions in multi-threaded environments automatically.
ConcreteState objects typically carry no instance-specific data — all domain data lives in the Context — so a single shared instance is safe and avoids allocation overhead.
JavaScript garbage collection cannot collect state objects unless they are singletons.
Singleton states allow the Context to compare states using === for transition detection.
quiz.explanation: State objects represent a configuration, not data. All the order data (id, total, customerId) stays in the Context. Since ConcreteStates are stateless, one instance serves all orders, eliminating allocation on every transition.

quiz.question: In the 'Context-driven' variant of the State pattern, where does the transition logic live?
options: Inside each ConcreteState's action methods, which call ctx.setState() directly.
In the client code that calls the Context's methods.
In a central transition table or map held by the Context, keyed on (currentState, event) → nextState.
In the State interface as default method implementations.
quiz.explanation: Context-driven implementations keep a transition table in the Context — { pendingState: { pay: paidState, cancel: cancelledState }, ... }. ConcreteStates only execute behaviour; the Context determines the next state from the table.

quiz.question: When should you use XState (or a similar statechart library) instead of a hand-rolled State pattern?
options: Whenever you have more than one state.
Only when building React applications.
When you need parallel states, nested (hierarchical) states, history pseudo-states, serialization, or visualization tooling — features that hand-rolled classes do not support cleanly.
Only when the application is deployed to production — XState is too heavy for development.
quiz.explanation: Hand-rolled State pattern is ideal for 3–6 simple states. XState adds parallel regions, hierarchical states, history, guards as pure functions, devtools visualization, and serializable snapshots — capabilities that scale to complex real-world workflows.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a real-world example of the State pattern?
options: A sorting library that supports bubble sort and quick sort interchangeably.
A pub/sub event bus that notifies multiple subscribers of changes.
The TCP/IP socket lifecycle (CLOSED → LISTEN → ESTABLISHED → TIME_WAIT) implemented in the operating system networking stack.
A factory method that returns different database adapters based on configuration.
quiz.explanation: TCP socket states are the canonical real-world State pattern example. Each state (LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, etc.) handles segments differently; illegal operations in a given state are handled per-state. Redux reducers with status fields and game AI FSMs are also textbook examples.

quiz.question: How does React's useReducer relate to the State pattern?
options: useReducer implements the Observer pattern — components observe state changes.

The reducer function is effectively a state machine: (currentState, action) => nextState. Dispatched action types are events, and the returned object is the new state — equivalent to a State pattern without explicit ConcreteState classes.
useReducer has no relationship to State — it is purely for performance optimisation.
useReducer implements the Command pattern — each dispatched action is a Command object.
quiz.explanation: useReducer is a functional state machine. The reducer maps (state, event) → nextState, exactly as a State machine transition function. Redux Toolkit's createAsyncThunk uses 'pending'/'fulfilled'/'rejected' status strings — the ConcreteState name equivalents in a data-driven implementation.
